newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian blue-chip shares pause to gather breath.
newsitem.headline: Indian blue-chip shares pause to gather breath.

text.p: An anticipated correction pulled shares down on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) on Friday after hitting a 33-month high the day before, but traders said the market was poised to rise again in the near term.
"The market is down today because of much needed correction," Jaswantlal Parekh, vice president of the BSE, told Reuters.
"The bull run will continue after the correction," he said.
"The undercurrent is still bullish," said Antony Sequeira, managing director of Arcadia Share & Stock Broking in Bombay.

The BSE 30-share benchmark index fell 57.23 points, or 1.31 percent, to 4,321.14 by the provisional close as operators unwound their long positions on the last day of the weekly settlement on the exchange.
The BSE index had hit a 33-month peak of 4,448.06 on Thursday, continuing a seven-week rally.
"Both markets are overbought," Sequeira said, referring to the BSE and the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
He expects the market to rise after Tuesday, the last day of account at the NSE.
Foreign institutional investors' (FIIs) purchases, which fuelled this month's boom, were continuing, he said.
Anand Jhaveri, head of broking at Birla Marlin Securities, said the BSE index could dip to the 4,000-level.
"The immediate top would be 4,500," he said. The index touched an all-time high of 4,643.31 points on September 12, 1994.
Some traders welcomed the fall in prices.
"The short-term correction is healthy for the market," said Govind Agarwal, head of sales at brokerage Motilal Oswal Securities.
Speculators who had bought shares, hoping to ride piggyback on the FIIs' buying wave, were selling. The FIIs had slowed purchases since Thursday, dealers said.
Analysts said the rise was fuelled by expectations of better corporate performances during the second half of 1997/98, good rains and reports of a pick-up in industrial production.
"The market is bullish as interest rates are falling and FIIs and NRIs (non-resident Indians) are putting money in stocks," said Parekh.
On Friday, NatWest Securities said the latest economic data suggested that an industrial revival was under way.

"Manufactured prices have started firming," NatWest economic analyst Anindya Chatterjee said. "Prices of cement, non-electrical machinery, drugs and medicines, cotton textiles have all moved up in April and May."
He said these developments reflected improved business activity and the emergence of trends that would stimulate business sentiment.
